items.prompt: Explain which fictional global-production offer better fits retained local livelihoods. A offers 100 local production jobs with limited training and uses some local suppliers. B offers 60 jobs, more advanced training and more local purchasing, but lower initial output. Both are funded and have buyers.
items.canonical_answer: A offers more immediate employment and a genuine local-supply link, which can support more households now. B develops deeper capabilities and retains more supplier spending, but creates fewer jobs initially. Prefer B where lasting skills and stronger local production links are the main priority; A may fit urgent broad employment needs better. Compare job quality, retained spending and future opportunities rather than treating larger output or a foreign connection as proof of local benefit.
marking_guidance: Judgement: compare genuine benefits and costs against the stated aim.
Reason: develop each option using supplied evidence, weigh the trade-off, and give a conditional conclusion.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

Development: connect price, unchanged quantity and fixed payment needs [4].

items.prompt: Calculate (a) fictional annual goods balance with N$140 million exports and N$170 million imports [2]. Explain (b) whether N$40 million foreign investment makes it a goods surplus when those trade values stay unchanged [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) 140 - 170 = -30 million N$, a N$30 million goods deficit. (b) No: investment is a separate financial flow, so the deficit remains. It may help finance activity or payment needs, but a later trade effect needs evidence of changed exports or imports.
marking_guidance: Evidence: correct method, deficit and N$ million [2].
Meaning: distinguish the unchanged goods measure from new financing and bound later effects [4].
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.
